text:
My first paying customer signed up on a Tuesday. $29 a month. I stared at the Stripe email for a full minute.

Then I refunded him two days later.

Here's what happened. He signed up for the invoicing part, which worked. Then he tried recurring invoices, which I had shipped the week before and tested exactly once, on my own account, with one line item. His invoice had eleven line items and a discount. The total came out wrong. Not a little wrong. $400 wrong.

He emailed me, very politely, and asked if the number was supposed to look like that.

I fixed the bug in about twenty minutes. It was a rounding thing, the discount was applied per line and then again on the total. Easy fix. But the number had already gone to his client. He had to send a correction. That's embarrassing for him, and it was my fault, not his.

So I refunded him and told him the month was on me. He stayed. He is still a customer, eighteen months later, and he has sent me more bug reports than anyone else. Good ones. The kind with screenshots.

The lesson I took from it is not "test more", although sure, test more. The lesson is that the first customer is not a revenue event. It's a trust event. Twenty-nine dollars does not matter. What matters is whether he tells the next person that the guy behind this thing actually answers email.

I still have the refund receipt in a folder called "first." Anyway. Test your discounts.
title: I refunded my first paying customer

text:
I quit in March. It's September. Here is the honest version, not the launch-tweet version.

Revenue: $1,840 a month. That's 61 customers. I thought I would be at $5k by now. I was wrong by a lot, and the reason is that I spent April and May building things nobody had asked for. More on that below.

Time: I work less than I did at my job, and it feels like more. The difference is nobody tells me when I'm done. I had to invent that. Now I stop at 5. Not because I'm tired, because the work I do after 5 is bad and I end up deleting it the next morning.

Support: about 40 minutes a day. I answer everything myself, same day. People are shocked by this, which tells you something about every other tool they use.

What I got wrong. I built a Zapier integration, a team plan, and a dark mode before I had 20 customers. Zero people asked for any of them. Then one person asked for a PDF export and I pushed it off for a month because it seemed boring. It is now the most used feature in the app. The boring thing was the thing.

What I got right. I called every customer who cancelled. All 14 of them. Eleven picked up. The calls were ten minutes each and I learned more in those calls than in any amount of analytics.

Would I do it again? Yes. Would I do it the same way? No. I'd build the PDF export first and I'd stop at 5 from day one.

That's the update. Next one in six months, with real numbers again.
title: Six months solo, the honest version

text:
There's a specific feeling when you're about to build something nobody asked for. It feels like momentum. It isn't.

I know this because I've done it four times now, and I keep a list. The Zapier integration. The team plan. Dark mode. A Slack bot that posts when an invoice gets paid. Total time, about six weeks. Total customers who used any of them in the first month: three. One of those was me.

The pattern is always the same. I get bored with the core product. The core product is invoicing, and invoicing is not exciting. So my brain looks for something that is exciting, and dresses it up as strategy. "Teams will unlock a bigger market." Sure. There was no evidence for that. There was evidence for a PDF export. Eleven people had asked for it by email. I didn't build it because it was boring.

So here's the rule I use now, and it's embarrassingly simple. Before I build anything, I need three emails from three different people asking for it. Not upvotes. Emails. If I can't find three, I don't build it. I write it on the list and I go answer support instead.

This has killed about a dozen ideas in the last three months. Some of them were probably good. I don't care. The cost of a good idea I didn't build is small. The cost of six weeks on the wrong thing when you're alone is the whole quarter.

Three emails. That's it. That's the post.
title: The feature nobody asked for

text:
I called all 14 customers who cancelled this year.

Eleven picked up. Nobody was angry. Most of them were apologetic, which was strange.

Three things I heard more than once:
- "I stopped sending invoices" (not my problem to fix, but good to know)
- "I couldn't find the export button" (my problem, fixed in a day)
- "I forgot I was paying for it" (ouch, and also the most useful one)

The third one is the one I keep thinking about. If you forget you're paying for something, it means the thing never showed up in your week. I'd rather hear that on a call than see it as a number on a churn chart.

Ten minutes per call. Best use of two hours all month.

Month 6 numbers, because I said I'd post them.

MRR: $1,840
Customers: 61
Churn: 4 this month
Support: ~40 min a day, all me

I'm behind where I said I'd be. I said $5k. The gap is almost entirely April and May, when I built three features nobody asked for instead of the one feature eleven people asked for.

Not posting this for sympathy. Posting it because every founder update I read is either a rocket ship or a eulogy, and most of us are somewhere in the boring middle. This is the boring middle.

Next update in March. Real numbers again.

Unpopular opinion from someone who answers every support email himself: most "scale" problems are just founders who don't want to talk to customers.

I have 61 customers. I know maybe 40 of them by name. When one of them emails me about a bug, I fix the bug and I reply with what I changed. Takes 40 minutes a day.

At some point this stops working. I know. But that point is a lot further out than people think, and the stuff you learn before you get there is the stuff that makes the product worth scaling.

Anyway. Go answer your inbox.
